title: Ezra Reads, the People Understand
hookLine: learning to read a verse, a prayer, a page
carry: prayer counts in any language; hebrew opens it
tomorrow: two people, one text, and something rests between them. what?

cards: A form on a college portal asks you to rate your languages: reading, speaking, writing. Next to Hebrew, some people would have to write: by sound only.
They can read the letters aloud in a prayer book and not know what most of the words mean. So can you pray in a language you barely read? The Mishnah answers plainly: yes.

teach.b: It lists things that may be said in any language: the Shema, the prayer, the grace after meals. A prayer you understand counts. So why learn more Hebrew at all?

teach.h: EZRA READS; THEY GIVE THE SENSE.
teach.b: The book of Nehemiah tells of a day when Ezra read the Torah aloud to the people in Jerusalem, and readers explained it, giving the sense, so the people understood what they heard. Reading and understanding, together.
More Hebrew is how those two meet in one person.
You start with words you already say. Shalom: peace. Torah: teaching.
Emet: truth. Chesed: kindness. Lev: heart.
Five words, and a page of the prayer book begins to light up in places. A verse becomes something you hear, not only something you sound out. Nobody has to be fluent for that.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Mishnah says the Shema may be said in any language.
And still people keep learning Hebrew, a word at a time, because each word is a small way in.

how: Jewish prayer may be said in any language, and prayer books often print Hebrew beside a translation; some adults keep learning Hebrew a few words at a time, in classes or with a tutor.

o: understanding more Hebrew, a few words at a time
switching every prayer to Hebrew at once
speaking only Hebrew at home from now on

games.q: five words you already say — tap the pairs.

s: the Mishnah says the Shema may be said in any language

you have to be fluent in Hebrew before your prayers count

games.q: a friend in your study group prays only in English and says she feels like a fake. what does the Mishnah say?
o: the Shema and the prayer may be said in any language.
prayers count only in Hebrew, so she should stop until she learns.
English is fine for study, but never for the Shema.
games.why: Mishnah Sotah lists the Shema, the prayer and the grace after meals among what may be said in any language.

practice: Write five Hebrew words by hand, in English letters, each with its meaning: shalom, peace; Torah, teaching; emet, truth; chesed, kindness; lev, heart. Say each one once, out loud, as you write it.
If you know the Hebrew letters, write one word in them too.

wordCard.voice: More Hebrew: a few words at a time, until a verse, a prayer, a page is something you hear and understand, not only sound out.

carryVoice: Your line: prayer counts in any language, and Hebrew opens it, word by word. Shalom for now.

sources.ref: Mishnah Sotah 7:1 (these may be said in any language: the Shema, the prayer, the grace after meals, and others)
Nehemiah 8:1-8 (Ezra reads the Torah to the people; it is read distinctly and the sense is given, so they understand)
